Four questions that decide the code
Material decides the chapter for most goods: a cotton shirt and a polyester shirt have different codes. Include the main material in your search.
Machines and electronics are classified by their function. Search for what it does (“pump”, “charger”, “router”) rather than a brand or model name.
Parts often have their own lines, usually ending in “parts”. If you ship parts, add the word “parts” to your search.
Clothing is split between Chapter {0} (knitted) and Chapter {1} (woven). A T-shirt is usually knitted; a formal shirt is usually woven.

HSN (Harmonized System of Nomenclature) is the international system for classifying goods. The first {0} digits are the same worldwide; India adds {1} more to make the {2}-digit ITC(HS) or Customs Tariff code used on bills of entry, shipping bills and GST invoices.
Is the HSN code the same for import, export and GST?
The {0}-digit code is the same in the Customs Tariff and ITC(HS) for import and export. GST invoices usually show {1}, {2} or {3} digits depending on turnover, but they follow the same structure.
Why do I get several possible codes?

Many products can sound alike in words but fall in different chapters depending on material, function or whether they are parts. The finder shows every line that matches your words; the right one is the line whose full description, read with the chapter notes, fits your goods.
Can I rely on the code the finder suggests?

No. It is a starting point for guidance only. The code you declare is your responsibility, and a wrong code can cost you duty, penalties or export benefits. Ask a licensed customs broker to confirm, or apply for an advance ruling if the case is unclear.
What does Restricted or Prohibited mean?

This is the ITC(HS) import or export policy for the code. Free means no licence is needed under that policy. Restricted needs a DGFT authorisation or must meet conditions. Prohibited cannot be imported or exported. State trading means only notified state agencies may trade it.

Know your true cost per unit.
Pick your goods, add the invoice and your costs in India, and get the landed cost per unit with duty and IGST worked out from the tariff.

Landed cost is the full price of an imported good by the time it reaches your warehouse: the goods, freight and insurance, customs duty, IGST, port and clearance charges and transport. Divide it by the number of units to get the true cost per unit.
Is IGST part of my landed cost?
IGST is paid at import, but a registered business can usually claim it back as input tax credit. The wizard shows the cost both ways. Tick the box if you claim the credit and it shows the net cost.
Why does the freight box say {0} percent?

When freight is not known, customs adds {0} percent of the FOB value as freight and {1} percent as insurance to work out the assessable value. If you know your real freight and insurance, enter them and the duty becomes more accurate.
Which charges should I put in step {0}?

Terminal handling, the shipping line delivery order, CFS or ICD charges, your customs broker fee, transport to your warehouse and anything else you pay, such as testing or inspection. Your forwarder and broker can give you these figures before the ship arrives.

Is this a real bill of lading or air waybill?

No. It is a draft for checking only and is marked DRAFT on every page. Only the shipping line, NVOCC or airline (or its agent) issues the real document and its number. Use this to agree the details with your forwarder and buyer before that happens.
Why make a draft at all?

Most B/L amendments and air waybill corrections come from small typing errors: a wrong consignee address, a missing HS code, a container number with one digit out. Sending your forwarder a clean draft first saves amendment fees and delays at destination.
How does it check container and AWB numbers?

Container numbers are checked against the ISO {0} check digit. Air waybill numbers are checked with the IATA rule: the first {1} digits of the serial divided by {2} must leave the last digit as the remainder.
How is the chargeable weight worked out?

For each line we take the higher of the gross weight and the volume weight (length × width × height in cm ÷ {0}), rounded up to the next half kilo. Your airline or forwarder may use a different factor, so check their rate sheet.
